Poland’s Elektra Energia Announces Major Investment in Grid Expansion

Elektra Energia, a leading player in Poland’s electric utilities sector, has announced a significant investment in the country’s power grid infrastructure. The firm will allocate 1.2 billion złoty over the next three years to expand and modernize its transmission and distribution networks, with a strong focus on serving the rapidly growing regions of Silesia and Greater Poland.

The expansion, revealed at a press briefing in Katowice on Thursday, comes amid steady increases in electricity demand driven by industrial development and urban population growth. Company executives stated that the plan includes the construction of new high-voltage substations, upgrading of existing lines, and integration of advanced digital monitoring systems to improve reliability and efficiency.

“Poland’s energy landscape is evolving quickly, and the investments we make today are vital to meet tomorrow’s challenges,” said Tomasz Zieliński, CEO of Elektra Energia. “Our commitment is to deliver stable, secure power to households and businesses, while laying the groundwork for a smart and sustainable grid.”

According to data from the Polish Power Association, national electricity consumption grew by 3.1% in 2023, with projections suggesting continued upward trends as new manufacturing facilities are established and electric vehicle adoption rises. Local governments have welcomed the announcement, citing the potential for job creation and improved service quality.

“We are pleased to see proactive steps from Elektra Energia in strengthening our region’s energy backbone,” said Anna Maj, the mayor of Bytom. “Reliable electricity is essential for attracting investments and supporting the quality of life for our residents.”

Industry experts point to the importance of grid modernization as Poland transitions towards a more diversified energy mix. Michał Nowacki, an analyst at the Warsaw Institute for Energy Studies, noted that enhanced infrastructure will support the integration of renewable sources such as wind and solar, which are expected to play a greater role in the national grid over the coming decade.

The company’s investment plan also includes training programs for engineers and technicians, in partnership with technical universities in Poznań and Gliwice. “This is a forward-thinking approach that will not only benefit consumers but also strengthen the local workforce,” said Agata Pawłowska, spokesperson for the Polish Energy Workers Union.

Construction on the first phase is set to begin later this summer, with completion scheduled for 2027.
